big_idea: Workplace conflict is fundamentally an emotional event, not a rational one, which is why standard, purely logic-based conflict-resolution training often fails. Daoust offers a flexible toolkit of techniques rather than one rigid method, so readers can pick what fits their own style.

tool.label: The Aiki approach
tool.text: Named for the aikido principle of blending with an opponent's energy rather than meeting it head-on, this technique is framed as a way to defuse a conflict by working with the other person's emotional energy instead of resisting or escalating it.
tool.note: The Aiki tool and an accompanying worksheet are confirmed via the author's own site; the detailed step-by-step mechanics couldn't be independently verified beyond that, so treat specifics beyond blend-don't-resist as unconfirmed.

ideas.title: Conflict is emotional first
ideas.text: Daoust's core argument is that people mismanage conflict because they treat it as a logic problem when it's really an emotional one.

ideas.title: Two bad defaults
ideas.text: Most people oscillate between two ineffective patterns: demanding what they want and damaging the relationship, or avoiding conflict and giving up what they need.

ideas.title: A toolkit, not one method
ideas.text: Rather than a single framework, the book offers multiple selectable tools so readers can combine strategies that suit their personality.

ideas.title: Irrational beliefs fuel escalation
ideas.text: Companion material addresses distorted thinking patterns that intensify workplace conflict.

ideas.title: Forgiveness as a conflict tool
ideas.text: A dedicated resource in the toolkit treats forgiveness as a practical step for moving past a conflict, not just a moral nicety.

ideas.title: Built for the real workplace
ideas.text: Daoust illustrates concepts through workplace scenarios rather than abstract theory.

try_it: Before your next tense work conversation, name the emotion you're feeling, not just the issue, before you say anything.
Identify one recurring work conflict where you default to either over-demanding or avoiding, and write down what a middle path would look like.
Notice one irrational or catastrophizing thought during a conflict this week and write a more balanced version of it.
After a disagreement is resolved, deliberately practice a small act of letting go rather than replaying the grievance.
best_for: People whose conflict-resolution training hasn't stuck because it was too rational or scripted
Managers wanting emotional self-regulation tools for workplace friction
less_useful: Readers wanting a single, clearly defined step-by-step model, since this is explicitly a pick-what-fits toolkit
Anyone needing frameworks for large organizational disputes rather than individual emotional regulation

related.why: A more scripted, step-by-step system for the same high-stakes conversations
The bigger picture of how ordinary conflict escalates into something harder to defuse
